sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Brest uses simple, flat rules. According to the city's parking page, updated on 7 October 2026, on-street parking is paid 9:00 to 12:00 and 13:30 to 19:00 every day except Sunday and public holidays; the orange zone near the shops allows up to 3h30 for 25 euros and the green zone the whole day for 25 euros, and the post-parking charge is also 25 euros [0]. A stay of under 30 minutes is free once a day per vehicle in the orange and green zones, and in car parks the third hour is offered when paying for two [1]. The city counts about 1,000 free and 4,000 paid on-street spaces in the centre, plus 3,400 paid spaces in car parks, a total that does not match the car parks it lists, which add up to about 2,460 [4]. Its FAQ lists three car parks as free, although the city's open data lists one of them as paid; the sources conflict [2]. 250 pay machines accept cards, and apps can be used by the minute [3]. The city says 31% of delivery stops are made double-parked or in prohibited areas, based on a 2022 diagnostic [16].

Public transport is a main alternative. From 1 September 2026 tram line A runs about every 5.5 minutes at the afternoon peak and line B about every 7.5 minutes [17]. The city lists four park-and-ride sites at the entrances with 682 places in total, free to Bibus ticket holders [10], and Bibus says two more are to open, one temporarily at the hospital and one in 2027 [11].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The main project is the replacement of the Saint-Louis underground car park. The city plans to demolish and rebuild it, with clearing from January 2027 and delivery in the first quarter of 2029 at about 18 million euros, with subscribers using the new Glacis car park meanwhile [6]. Glacis, on rue Duquesne, has five levels and 215 spaces, cost 7.3 million euros and was inaugurated on 19 September 2026, with 45 spaces with EV chargers and secure bike parking for 44 bikes; the city said it would soon open to the general public, which we could not confirm [5]. Place de la Liberté was resurfaced from April to July 2026, partly to waterproof the underground car park below [7]. A secure bike car park was announced for the Coat-ar-Guéven car park from 20 July 2026 [8], and a 200-space car park opened by the commercial port in July 2026 with a free summer shuttle as a trial to 28 August [9].

For electric cars, a contractor is installing 15 on-street charging stations with 72 charge points, with first openings planned for summer 2026 and completion by mid-2027 [12]. The city's open data records EV charging spaces mostly at Les Glacis (45) [13].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The city names Brest'Park as manager of the new Glacis car park, with tariffs and hours published on its own site [15]. The city's open-data layer lists capacity, payment type and EV places for each car park but no occupancy, and is declared to be updated every five years [14]. We found no source on the operating contracts or resident subscription prices.

Our data cover seven car parks with 2,366 spaces from the city's live feed, measured since 5 October 2026: Coat-ar-Guéven (690 in the feed against 720 on the city page), Les Capucins (630), Liberté (450), Jaurès (400), Château (81), Gares (75) and Sangnier (40). Occupancy averaged about 36% on weekdays and 31% at weekends, weighted by spaces. The busiest of the big garages is Liberté at 57% on weekdays, followed by Jaurès at 37% and Coat-ar-Guéven at 33%. Les Capucins is the quietest at 19% on weekdays, though it is the only large garage that is busier at weekends (25%) and reached 82% on a Sunday afternoon. The small surface car parks fill: Gares averaged 68% on weekdays and reached full in a single reading on a Thursday afternoon. Glacis does not appear in our feed. These are about two weeks of data.
